1114.title: Waking the Goddess Early
1114.hook: night six: Bengal wakes the goddess out of season, the way Rama once did

1114.howItsDone: In Bengal, Durga Puja begins with bodhon, the awakening of the goddess, on the sixth evening; the autumn worship is called akal bodhan, the untimely awakening, after Rama's worship before his battle, and at Sandhi Puja 108 lotuses are offered. Where the nine forms are kept, the sixth night honors Katyayani.

segments.voice: Drums, big ones, slung on the shoulder, and the sound carries down the lane. In Kolkata and across Bengal, around this point in the nights, Durga Puja gets under way. Inside a decorated tent called a pandal stands a clay goddess with many arms, a lion at her feet and the buffalo demon under her spear, her four children beside her. And on this sixth evening, before anything else, the priests do something that sounds strange. They wake her up.
screen: `DRUMS DOWN THE LANE.` → `A GODDESS WITH HER CHILDREN.` → `TONIGHT: WAKE HER UP.`

segments.voice: Where the nine forms are kept, the sixth night belongs to Katyayani, named, the story says, for the sage Katyayana. In Bengal the sixth evening has its own rite: bodhon, the awakening. Tradition says the gods rest through the southern half of the year, and autumn falls inside it. The goddess's older, timely worship is in spring; Bengal still keeps it as Basanti Puja. The autumn festival is called akal bodhan, the untimely awakening, and the Bengali Ramayana of Krittivas tells how it began. Rama is about to fight Ravana to bring Sita home, and he needs the goddess now, not in spring. He gathers a hundred and eight blue lotuses for the offering, and counting them out, he finds one missing. The goddess has hidden it, to test him. People called Rama lotus-eyed. So he takes up an arrow to offer one of his own eyes in place of the flower. Before he can, she appears, stops his hand, and blesses him to win. That's the teaching under the drums, and its name is bhakti, devotion, at full strength. The goddess isn't kept by a calendar. She answers a heart that holds nothing back. So Bengal's festival begins by calling her awake, and at Sandhi Puja, as the eighth day turns into the ninth, a hundred and eight lotuses are offered in memory of Rama's. Earlier this year you met her as Uma, the daughter coming home. Tonight is how she's called. And that's the comfort for a busy life now: you don't wait for the right season, or the perfect day, to turn to God. A whole heart is the right time.
screen: `KATYAYANI, THE SIXTH NAME.` · `BODHON: THE AWAKENING.` · `AKAL BODHAN: CALLED OUT OF SEASON.` · `108 LOTUSES, ONE MISSING.` · `RAMA OFFERS HIS EYE.` · then, large: `DEVOTION WAKES THE GODDESS.`

segments.voice: Hold a flower if one is near, or cup your empty hands as if you held one, the way people do at pushpanjali, the flower offering at Durga Puja. Bring what Rama brought: not a perfect time, just a whole heart. Then offer it. If you pray, you can say Om Durgayai namah, salutations to Durga, or use your own words. If you don't, offer the flower to the one thing you most want to give yourself to fully this week.

1115.title: Why the Books Rest
1115.hook: night seven: the fierce Kalaratri arrives, and in many homes the schoolbooks are laid before Saraswati to rest
1115.carry: learning is sacred: the book is Saraswati's
1115.tomorrow: why do grown-ups wash little girls' feet?
1115.howItsDone: In many Hindu homes, especially in South India, books, pens and instruments are placed before Saraswati in the last days of Navaratri and not used until Vijayadashami, when they are taken up with a blessing and small children begin to write (vidyarambham); a dropped book is touched to the forehead. Where the nine forms are kept, the seventh night honors Kalaratri.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, night six, Bengal's line: akal bodhan, devotion wakes the goddess. Rama would have given his own eye.
screen: `DEVOTION WAKES THE GODDESS.` · `NIGHT SEVEN.`

segments.voice: A schoolbook, a pen, a harmonium, a child's slate. In some homes, around this point in Navaratri, they're stacked together in front of an image of Saraswati, the goddess of learning, music and speech, and decorated with a little sandal paste and a flower. Then nobody touches them: no homework from those books, no practice on that instrument, until the festival is over. In the three-by-three way of keeping the festival, Saraswati's nights begin about now. But the seventh name in the Kavacha's list is not gentle at all.
screen: `BOOKS STACKED BEFORE SARASWATI.` → `NOBODY TOUCHES THEM.` → `THE SEVENTH NAME IS NOT GENTLE.`

segments.voice: Her name is Kalaratri. You can hear ratri in it, night, the same word that's in Navaratri. In paintings of this night she's black as a moonless sky, hair loose and wild, breath like fire, sometimes riding a donkey. And yet devotees who keep the nine forms give her a second name, Shubhankari, the one who does good. Hindus come back to that idea again and again: the fierce form of the goddess is the protecting one. Her terror points at whatever would harm her children, never at them. Now the books. In homes that keep it, especially in the South, the last days of Navaratri turn to Saraswati, and the tools of learning are set before her: schoolbooks, pens, a harmonium, a child's slate. The reason is a belief most Hindu kids learn early. Knowledge isn't just information. It belongs to Saraswati; it's a form of the goddess herself. That's why a Hindu child who steps on a book, or drops one, picks it up and touches it to the forehead, a small sorry. For these days the books rest. Then on the tenth day they're picked up with a blessing, and in Kerala and other places small children write their first letters, often traced in a plate of rice, a rite called vidyarambham, the beginning of learning. So night seven sets two faces of one goddess side by side: the dark one who guards, and the bright one who teaches. Learning isn't only something you use. It's something you bow to.

segments.voice: Pick up a book near you, any book, or the phone you read on, and hold it for a moment the way a Hindu child does after dropping one: touch it lightly to your forehead. 1116.title: The Goddess at the Table
1116.hook: night eight: Mahagauri, the bright one, and young girls are welcomed in, their feet washed, and served as the goddess
1116.carry: the goddess dwells in every being
1116.tomorrow: why would a mechanic garland his wrenches?
1116.howItsDone: In parts of North India, families keep kanya puja (kanjak) on the eighth or ninth day of Navaratri, washing the feet of young girls, feeding them puri, halwa and chickpeas, and giving them small gifts; where the nine forms are kept, the eighth night honors Mahagauri.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SIXTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, night seven: learning is sacred, the book is Saraswati's, and fierce Kalaratri guards it.
screen: `LEARNING IS SOMETHING YOU BOW TO.` · `NIGHT EIGHT.`

segments.voice: The doorbell rings, and it's the girls from down the street, a little shy, in their best clothes. Inside, the grown-ups have been cooking since early: puris, a sweet semolina halwa, spiced chickpeas. The girls sit in a row. An aunt kneels and washes their feet, dabs a red mark on each forehead, ties a red thread on each wrist. They're served first, before anyone else eats, and they leave with a small gift. In parts of North India this is kanya puja, or kanjak, kept on the eighth or ninth day. For a morning, the goddess is the girl next door.
screen: `THE GIRLS FROM DOWN THE STREET.` → `FEET WASHED, SERVED FIRST.` → `THE GODDESS NEXT DOOR.`

segments.voice: The eighth name in the Kavacha's list is Mahagauri. It means the great Gauri, and Gauri is a name of Parvati, the bright one. On this night she's shown dressed in white, calm, shining. There's a story people tell about it. Parvati did hard austerities for a long time to win Shiva, out in the sun and the rain, until her body was darkened with dust and weather. When Shiva finally accepted her, he washed her with the water of the Ganga, and she came out shining. So the bright form is what's left after long effort, washed clean. Now hold that next to the morning with the girls. Usually children touch their elders' feet. In kanya puja the elders wash the children's feet, and the aunts and grandmothers serve the girls first. Behind it is one of the best-known hymns of the Devi Mahatmya, one many families chant in these nights. The gods praise the goddess who dwells in all beings: as consciousness, as sleep, as hunger, as mercy, as mother. And each time they bow, again and again. That's the teaching kanya puja acts out. The goddess isn't only in the temple or on the altar. She dwells in every being, and for one morning a house practices seeing her in the smallest people at its table. Mahagauri is brightness after long effort. Kanya puja is learning to see that brightness in a child.
screen: `MAHAGAURI, THE GREAT BRIGHT ONE.` · `WASHED CLEAN AFTER LONG EFFORT.` · `THE ELDERS WASH THE GIRLS' FEET.` · `SHE DWELLS IN ALL BEINGS.` · then, large: `THE GODDESS AT YOUR TABLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a child or a young person you know, a niece, a neighbor's kid, a student, your own, and see their face. Instead of the usual thoughts, homework, screen time, behavior, look at them the way the aunts look at the girls at kanya puja: as someone worth serving, with the goddess living in them. If you pray, you can quietly say the hymn's refrain over them, namas tasyai, salutations to her, or hold them before God in your own words. If you don't, simply wish them well by name.

1117.howItsDone: In parts of South India, Ayudha Puja on the ninth day of Navaratri honors tools, vehicles, machines and instruments, which are cleaned, decorated and rested; where the nine forms are kept, the ninth night honors Siddhidatri, and the next day is Vijayadashami.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, night eight: the goddess dwells in every being, served in young girls at the table. Tonight, the last night.
screen: `THE GODDESS AT YOUR TABLE.` · `NIGHT NINE.`

segments.voice: An auto-rickshaw parked outside a temple, with a garland of marigolds across its windshield and a smear of turmeric on the bumper. A mechanic's shop where the wrenches have been wiped clean, laid in a row and given a flower each. A tailor's sewing machine with a red dot on it. A laptop, closed, with a sprig of something green on the lid. In parts of South India, the ninth day of Navaratri is Ayudha Puja, the worship of tools. Where it's kept, the tools aren't worked with today. They're cleaned, thanked and honored.
screen: `A GARLAND ON THE WINDSHIELD.` → `A FLOWER ON EACH WRENCH.` → `TOOLS CLEANED AND HONORED.`

segments.voice: The ninth name in the Kavacha's list, the last one, is Siddhidatri, the giver of siddhi: accomplishment, the power to bring a thing to completion. On this night she's shown seated on a lotus, calm. Now put her beside the mechanic. Where does accomplishment come from? Hindus have an old answer, near the end of the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna says a person reaches siddhi, the same word, by worshiping the one from whom all beings come, through their own work. Not by leaving the shop for the temple. By the work itself, offered. That's the teaching Ayudha Puja acts out once a year. The wrench, the sewing machine, the pen, the stove, the laptop are how a life serves, so for a day they're cleaned, rested and honored like anything else on an altar. Look back over the nine nights. The goddess came as the mountain's daughter, a smile that made a world, a mother with her child, a warrior named for a sage, night itself, the bright one washed clean, and now the giver of accomplishment. And remember night one. Near the end of the Devi Mahatmya, the goddess herself speaks of the great worship offered to her in autumn, and says that whoever hears her story then, with devotion, will be freed from troubles by her grace. Tomorrow the year turns to Shiva, and to the Shiva Purana.
screen: `SIDDHIDATRI, GIVER OF ACCOMPLISHMENT.` · `THE GITA: SIDDHI THROUGH YOUR OWN WORK.` · `THE TOOLS REST ON THE ALTAR.` · `THE AUTUMN WORSHIP AND THE BOOK.` · then, large: `WORK OFFERED IS WORSHIP.`

segments.voice: One by one, bring to mind the things your hands use to get through a day, keys, a phone, a pan, a pen, a keyboard, a steering wheel, a broom, and give each a moment of thanks, the way the mechanic gives each wrench a flower. Then let the hands themselves come to mind, resting in your lap; they're tools too. If you pray, you can offer tomorrow's work to the goddess, or to God, in your own words. If you don't, simply decide to do one piece of it well, as a gift.

segments.voice: Yesterday: work offered to God becomes worship, and the goddess's part of the year closed. Today the year turns to Shiva.

segments.voice: Two gods are arguing. Brahma, the creator, says he's the greatest, since everything came from him. Vishnu, the preserver, says no, he is, since he keeps everything going. The argument gets hot. Then, between the two of them, a pillar of fire appears, blazing, going up past where they can see and down past where they can see. No top in sight, and no bottom. Both gods stop mid-sentence. You heard this on Shivaratri, back on day ninety; today it comes from the Shiva Purana itself.
screen: `TWO GODS ARGUING.` → `A PILLAR OF FIRE.` → `NO TOP, NO BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: The Shiva Purana is a big book of Shiva's stories, told aloud by a storyteller named Suta to a gathering of sages; the path takes selections. The two gods agree on a test: whoever finds the end of this thing wins. Vishnu becomes a boar and digs down. Brahma becomes a swan and flies up. Vishnu finds no bottom, and finally comes back and says so. Brahma finds no top. But on the way he meets a ketaki flower drifting down, and he has an idea. He comes back, says he reached the top, and brings the flower along to swear it's true. Then the pillar opens and Shiva steps out of it. He honors Vishnu for telling the truth and rebukes Brahma for the lie, and in the story the ketaki flower, the false witness, is not to be offered in Shiva's worship. Linga means a mark, a sign. For Shaiva devotees, the linga in a Shiva temple recalls this pillar, and that's why the main image in so many Shiva temples has no face and no arms: it's a sign of what can't be measured, God with no top and no bottom, beyond every form. Temple walls carve the moment, Shiva stepping out of the pillar, the boar below, the swan above; it's called Lingodbhava. And the one who comes out well is the one who admitted it: I couldn't find the end. Before God that big, the story honors the honest answer.
screen: `A BOOK OF SHIVA'S STORIES.` · `A BOAR DIGS, A SWAN FLIES.` · `ONE ADMITS IT, ONE LIES.` · `LINGA: A SIGN OF THE UNMEASURED.` · then, large: `NO TOP. NO BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one big question you have no answer to and let it stand in front of you like the pillar, too big to measure. Let any quick answer drift by, like the flower. Then do what devotees do at a Shiva temple, in your mind or with a cup of water at the sink: pour a little water, slowly, as if over the linga. If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya, bowing to Shiva, or the name of God you use. If you don't, let the water run and say: I don't know the end of this, and that's honest.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Shiva Purana, the pillar of fire. The linga: a sign of the God beyond measure.
screen: `NO TOP. NO BOTTOM.` · `THE LINGA: GOD BEYOND MEASURE.`

segments.voice: From Kailash, Sati sees them go by in the sky: gods and their wives, dressed for a celebration, heading to her father's house. Daksha, her father, is holding a great sacrifice, a yajna, and the guests are streaming in. Everyone, it seems, except Sati and her husband. Daksha has left out his own son-in-law, Shiva. Sati turns to her husband and says she wants to go. A family quarrel that shakes the world.
screen: `GUESTS IN THE SKY.` → `EVERYONE BUT SHIVA.` → `SATI WANTS TO GO.`

segments.voice: The grudge is old. At an earlier gathering of the gods, Daksha walked in and the others rose to honor him, but Shiva stayed seated. Daksha never forgave it. To him, Shiva was an embarrassment: smeared with ash, wandering cremation grounds. Shiva warns Sati not to go uninvited, but surely her own family won't turn her away. She goes, and it's worse than he said. There's no portion set aside for Shiva at all. Her father greets her coldly and scorns her husband before everyone. Sati rebukes her father before the gods, and then, the story says, she gives up her body by the power of her own yoga, rather than live as the daughter of the man who mocked Shiva. Shiva's grief becomes fury. From his matted hair he brings out Virabhadra, a terrible warrior, who wrecks the sacrifice. Daksha is killed. When the gods beg, Shiva relents, and Daksha lives again with a goat's head: a proud man, humbled. Now the teaching. Daksha's ritual was flawless. What he left out was the Lord. Many teachers read Daksha as pride itself, the ego that can sit right inside religion, getting every detail right and shutting God out. And look at what he mocked: the ash. To this day Shiva's devotees wear sacred ash, vibhuti, often as three lines across the forehead. Many say it's a reminder: the body ends in ash, and only God remains. Read with Daksha, pride ends in ash too. So today, when you catch yourself looking down on someone, or getting every detail right while leaving God out, remember the ash. If this story stirs thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.
screen: `AN OLD GRUDGE AT A GATHERING.` · `SATI GOES ANYWAY.` · `A PERFECT RITUAL, AND NO SHIVA.` · `A GOAT'S HEAD AND A SECOND CHANCE.` · `VIBHUTI: THE ASH, WORN.` · then, large: `WHAT DAKSHA MOCKED, DEVOTEES WEAR.`

segments.voice: Many Shiva devotees start the day by drawing sacred ash across the forehead in three lines, saying Om Namah Shivaya. Try the gesture now, with or without ash. If you don't, simply say: this too goes to ash.

1120.hook: spring arrives on Shiva's mountain out of season, and Kama, the god of desire, takes aim at the god who is deep in meditation

1120.tomorrow: how will Parvati win the god who burned desire?
1120.howItsDone: Hindus tell the burning of Kama in the Shiva Purana and in poetry and dance; Shiva is often shown with a third eye on his forehead, and in some places the story is remembered at Holi or in spring festivals.

segments.voice: On a frozen mountainside, the snow starts to melt. Out of season, trees burst into flower. Bees show up, a cuckoo sings, the breeze turns warm and sweet. Every living thing on the mountain feels it, except one. Under a tree, Shiva sits in meditation, perfectly still, eyes closed, as if spring were somebody else's business. Behind a bush, with a bow made of sugarcane and arrows tipped with flowers, crouches Kama, the god of desire. He's been sent on a mission, and he's nervous.
screen: `SPRING, OUT OF SEASON.` → `SHIVA, PERFECTLY STILL.` → `KAMA TAKES AIM.`

segments.voice: Here's why he's there. Since Sati gave up her body, Shiva has withdrawn into meditation. Sati has been born again as Parvati, the daughter of the mountain king, and she comes every day to serve him: flowers, water, a clean place to sit. He doesn't look up. Meanwhile a demon named Taraka has a boon, and in the Shiva Purana only a son of Shiva can defeat him. So the gods need Shiva to marry, and Shiva is busy being still. Indra, king of the gods, sends Kama, and Spring with him. Kama waits for his moment, Parvati standing near, and lets an arrow fly. For a moment it works. Shiva's mind stirs; he opens his eyes and looks at Parvati. Then he catches himself, looks for the cause, and sees Kama with his bow. Fire bursts from Shiva's third eye, and Kama is burned to ash on the spot. You met this at Holi, on day ninety-six; here is how the book tells it. Rati, Kama's wife, falls weeping beside the ashes, and she's promised her husband will live again. Now, what Hindus take from it is not that desire is bad. Kama, desire and pleasure, is one of the four purusharthas, the aims of a human life, alongside dharma, doing right, artha, making a living, and moksha, freedom. But Shiva is the great yogi, and many read the third eye as the eye of wisdom: desire that tries to command him burns. And Kama doesn't vanish. From then on he's called Ananga, the bodiless one, love moving everywhere unseen. Whatever wins Shiva will have to come from Parvati herself. That closes a week full of fire.
screen: `PARVATI SERVES; SHIVA IS STILL.` · `THE GODS SEND DESIRE.` · `THE THIRD EYE OPENS.` · `KAMA: ONE OF LIFE'S FOUR AIMS.` · `ANANGA, THE BODILESS.` · then, large: `AN AIM OF LIFE, NEVER THE MASTER.`

segments.voice: Sit as still as you comfortably can, and sooner or later a want will show up: to check your phone, to eat, to be somewhere else. Don't fight it or obey it; notice it, watch it rise and fall like spring around a still figure under a tree, and come back to the breath. If you pray, you can say Om Namah Shivaya, or the name of God you use, each time you come back.
The Shiva Purana. Today: Kama burned by the third eye, and living on as Ananga.
